I think you missed the main point of religious ethics (and also, and not coincidentally, the main point of moral realism, though you don't mention it here).

To this you might reply, “But how can we know how to live without religion?”

That isn't really the concern. I know that's how people generally frame it, but I don't believe it's accurate. They aren't really concerned about how they would know how to live - they've already mostly worked that out. What they're really concerned about is being able to claim legitimacy when they attempt to impose their ideas of how to live on other people.

The real value of religion in this context (and of moral realism) isn't to have a purportedly objective basis upon which to make ones own decisions, but to have a purportedly objective basis upon which to claim the right to impose ones preferences on others. It saves people from having to try to claim, "You must do that because I say so." They can instead claim, "You must do that because God says so," or "You must do that because the universe says so."

More broadly, I think you do your message a disservice by focusing on religion. Religion isn't really the problem per se - it's simply the most significant and common instance of the problem (and it's noteworthy that, in the western world at least, it's becoming less significant and common, but the problem isn't going away - if anything, it's becoming even more widespread). The real problem is the nexus of dogmatism and authoritarianism - the rigid attachment to a particular narrow set of norms and the bland presumption that those norms, whatever they are, are, for whatever reason, so certainly valid that everyone else should rightly be forced to submit to them.

I don't believe it's a coincidence, for instance, that the social justice movement has arisen, and particularly among the young, just as religious faith has dropped off. I see it really as just a somewhat different expression of the same basic dynamic - the same absolute faith in a narrow set of beliefs, the same characterization of all who might not wholly agree as evil heretics, the same self-righteous fervor, the same harsh judgmentalism, the same irrationality and destructiveness.

I would say that there's a deeper and more fundamental issue, and religion is just historically the most notable expression of it, and it's that deeper and more fundamental issue that really needs to be drug out into the light.

That said, I agree with most of what you say here. I just think your focus is a bit too narrow.
